title: What "Enough" Feels Like, at 18 and 48
author: Eyal, Nir
summary: Nir Eyal and his 18-year-old daughter Jasmine co-write a father-daughter dialogue exploring why nothing ever feels like 'enough,' moving through three stages: chasing a single goal that will supposedly complete you, discovering that no amount of achievement satisfies for long, and finally landing on the idea that life is the pursuit of the next 'enough.' Jasmine's stories, from an obsessively planned tenth-birthday party to anxiety over college admissions, mirror Nir's own experience chasing business success after his MBA, both illustrating how tying happiness to outcomes outside one's control guarantees disappointment. Their resolution, borrowed from Nir's WISE goals framework, is to define 'enough' in terms that are entirely within one's own control, reframing the pursuit as a trail with resting points rather than a single mountain to summit.
points: Tying happiness to outcomes outside your control (a party going perfectly, an admissions decision) guarantees disappointment, since the outcome was never fully within reach.
Achieving a long-desired goal (an MBA, a company launch) rarely feels like 'enough' for long — the goalposts move as soon as they're reached.
Reframe 'enough' using the WISE goals framework: set goals defined by what's within your control, not by outcomes others control.
View 'enough' as a trail with resting points to acknowledge progress, not a single mountain summit that ends the pursuit once reached.
Wanting more isn't inherently a flaw — it's part of human nature and drives flourishing — the fix is aiming that instinct at controllable goals.
quotes: I tied so much of my success to an outcome that I had little control over.
as soon as you reached what you thought would be “enough,” it changed, and you were constantly chasing a moving target.
Instead of viewing “enough” as a mountain you climb, and when you reach the top you’re done, it’s more of a trail.
I will never, no matter what I have or do, feel like it’s “enough.” My demands, needs, and expectations are a constantly moving target.
It’s funny because the things you dream of change over time, but that blinding feeling of wanting something never goes away.
